# **000-Abstracto** {#000-abstracto}

The goal of this project is to develop a web application that helps identify the original publisher of a real estate listing on the internet. The user provides a link to a housing advertisement, and the system extracts key information such as price, surface area, location, and images. Using this data, the application searches for the same property across multiple real estate portals, agency websites, and private listings, grouping all matching advertisements into a single unified result.

The system builds a timeline based on verified publication dates to determine which listing appeared first. This makes it possible to identify whether the original publisher is a private owner or a real estate agent, and to distinguish them from intermediaries who later replicated the same advertisement. The result is a ranked list showing the original source first, followed by all subsequent copies with their respective publication dates.

This project aims to increase transparency in the real estate market and reduce unnecessary intermediaries. From a technical perspective, it involves web scraping, database storage, comparison algorithms, and potentially image or location matching to recognize the same property across different platforms. The tool is designed as a B2B solution for real estate professionals, helping them save time, avoid duplicate work, and contact the correct party directly.

# **001-Búsqueda de información** {#001-búsqueda-de-información}

##  **001-Identificar empresas representativas**  {#001-identificar-empresas-representativas}

As of now, i have not found a company that does the same as what i want to do with this project. With both my experience in the sector and a large amount of recent research I have to conclude that this is a new kind of project that I am starting. The closest that I have been able to come to this idea, company wise, are companies like Idealita and Fotocasa. They also have search engines for real estate ads, but they don't show which ad was made first, nor do they have a function to group similar ads for ease of finding the original. 

##  **002-Estructura de las empresas**  {#002-estructura-de-las-empresas}

FirstListing is designed as a small technology startup developing a web-based system for analyzing and clustering real estate listings. The company structure depends on the project’s scale. In the realistic version, it operates as a micro-enterprise with one founder. The founder acts as both CEO and technical lead, handling strategy, programming, database design, data processing, and client communication. 

The structure is flat, with fast decision-making and low complexity. If hypothetically scaled to 5–7 people, the company would be divided into functional areas such as leadership (CEO/Product Owner), backend development, frontend development, data engineering, and infrastructure management. This shows that the company size must match the scope and complexity of the product.

##  **003-Características de los departamentos**  {#003-características-de-los-departamentos}

FirstListing is mainly a software company, so development is the core department from day one. In the initial stage, the founder handles development, product design, basic marketing, and basic accounting internally.

Tax management and legal advice are outsourced from the beginning to ensure compliance and reduce risk.

During the first year, the structure remains lean, with most advanced services subcontracted. Within five years, if the company grows, marketing and customer management could become internal roles, and development could expand into separate backend and frontend positions. In ten years, all key departments—development, marketing, and administration—could be fully internalized, depending on growth.

##  **004-Funciones de cada departamento**  {#004-funciones-de-cada-departamento}

The development department builds and maintains the software. It manages the database, improves the system, and ensures the platform works correctly. The marketing function studies market needs, explains the value of the product, and attracts potential clients.

The administration function manages billing, payments, and basic accounting. Tax management is outsourced to ensure legal compliance. If the company grows, customer support and infrastructure management could become separate roles. All departments work together so the technical, commercial, and financial areas support each other.

##  **005-Evaluación del volumen de negocio**  {#005-evaluación-del-volumen-de-negocio}

FirstListing targets a niche but real market that I have experienced personally, within the real estate sector. At a local and regional level, there are thousands of agencies that publish listings online and face issues with duplicated properties due to portals, XML feeds, and co-brokering. At a national level in Spain, the addressable market is limited to a fraction of all agencies, but still represents several thousand potential professional users. Theoretically it could also be used by private users. Internationally, I believe the same problem exists, but expansion would need to happen country by country due to different portals and market structures. The Spanish real estate market is also extraordinarily disorganised, which is great for the national view.

A realistic market share for FirstListing is modest, as it is a specialized B2B tool rather than a mass-market product. However, even a small percentage of adoption within the addressable market would be enough to justify the project, especially because duplicate detection alone already provides clear value. Based on this, the project makes sense to continue in its current direction, with any future pivot more likely to be an extension of the concept rather than a complete change. 

The plan is to start with the real estate market on Costa Blanca south. Here I know that there are roughly 850-900 different real estate companies, mostly catering to foreigners. 

Behind this analysis there is concrete data that helps explain why the project is realistic. In Costa Blanca South there are around 850–900 active real estate agencies. If FirstListing is priced at about 30 € per month, one agent would pay 360 € per year. If only 10 % of the agencies use the tool, that would be around 90 agents and an annual revenue of roughly 32,400 €. If adoption reaches 25 %, that would be about 225 agents and around 81,000 € per year. These numbers are based on simple, realistic assumptions and show that even with low adoption, the project can generate meaningful revenue. This makes it possible to evaluate the project using real figures rather than speculation and to decide later whether scaling or adjusting the idea is necessary.

##  **007-Valoración de recursos humanos y materiales**  {#007-valoración-de-recursos-humanos-y-materiales}

To launch FirstListing, a few resources must be considered.

Even if the company starts as a one-person business, a realistic annual salary must be assigned. If we say that the salaries will be a gross annual cost of 24,000€, this represents the minimum personnel expense.

Material costs for the first year would include: computer equipment (1,500€), server hosting and cloud services (500€–1,000€), and utilities such as internet, electricity, and software tools (approximately 250€ per month \= 3,000€ per year). If operating from home (telework), office rent would be 0€. A realistic estimate of total material costs would be around 7,000€–7,500€ in the first year. In the second it would be less, unless we needed more because of growing.

Total estimated first-year costs:  
24,000€ (salary) \+ 7,500€ (materials) ≈ 31,500€.

Now we estimate income.

If FirstListing is priced at 30€ per month (360€ per year per client), the company would need approximately 88 paying clients in the first year to cover 31,500€ in costs (31,500 / 360 ≈ 88).

In the local market of around 900 agencies, this represents almost 10% market penetration in the first year, which is ambitious. A more realistic scenario might be 40–60 clients in year one, generating 14,400€–21,600€, meaning a first-year loss.

FirstListing would likely not be profitable in year one unless adoption exceeds expectations- or if i could do it much cheaper or without a pay. I don't need a full salary, since I wouldn't be working on it full time. Therefore it could be possible, even though these calculations are a more realistic scenario.

##  **008-Realización de seguimiento**  {#008-realización-de-seguimiento}

In this project, I started from the ground up rather than following a strict predefined plan, which may not have been the most time-efficient approach, but it made sense given the nature of the work — roughly 95% of the project is database logic, so that's where I focused first.

My timeline looked roughly like this:

Week 1-2: I began by sketching out the database structure on paper — how the different components should relate to each other and what data needed to flow where. I also created a very basic SQL database and rough, initial code for both the crawler and the parser.

Week 1-7 (first month and a half): Rather than moving linearly through stages, I worked in continuous iterations. I repeatedly refined and improved the parser, then the crawler, then both together. Over this period, I built four or five different versions of the crawler before settling on a final version that worked reliably. For the parser, I went through two or three major iterations before deciding on the final version, which used the OpenAI API — that was ultimately the only approach that worked effectively for the data extraction and comparison logic.

SQL Database: I only needed to create two versions of the SQL database since it wasn't particularly complex once I had the core structure right.

Week 7-10 (final 2-3 weeks): Only at the very end did I work on the frontend — HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

In total, the project spanned roughly two and a half months, worked on intermittently throughout.

##  **009-Desarrollo sostenible**  {#009-desarrollo-sostenible}

Since FirstListing is a digital product, its environmental impact is mainly related to server energy consumption and data storage. It does not require physical production or transport, its footprint is relatively low. However, hosting, data processing, and crawling still consume electricity. And getting the materials to build data centers also has an environmental impact.

To improve sustainability, the company can use efficient code, reduce unnecessary data storage, limit crawling frequency, and choose hosting providers powered by renewable energy. Overall, the impact is mainly digital and can be minimized through responsible technical decisions.

# **002-Selección de un servicio o producto** {#002-selección-de-un-servicio-o-producto}

##  **001-Identificar las necesidades**  {#001-identificar-las-necesidades}

In my work in the real agency, I have noticed that it is often difficult to know whether a property listing is truly the original one or simply a copy that has been republished by other agencies or portals. It is very common to see the same property repeated on several websites with the same photos and very similar information, but with small differences such as the price, the description, or the contact person. This makes the market confusing and makes it easy to waste time trying to find which version is the “real” one.

This problem does not only affect professionals, but also buyers, because if it is not clear who published the property first, it is possible to end up dealing with intermediaries who only replicate the listing. If it were possible to quickly detect which listing is the original and who actually manages it, a lot of time could be saved and, in some cases, also money. For this reason, the main need behind this project is to make the process more transparent and to avoid the repetitive work of manually comparing listings across different portals.

##  **002-Plantear posibles soluciones**  {#002-plantear-posibles-soluciones}

A possible solution to this problem would be to develop a web application that helps identify the original publisher of a real estate listing on the internet. The user could provide a link to a housing advertisement, and the system extracts key information such as price, surface area, location, images and description. Using this data, the application searches for the same property across multiple real estate portals, agency websites, and private listings, grouping all matching advertisements into a single unified result. When we then have this list of properties that hopefully is the same property, we can build a timeline based on verified publication dates to determine which listing appeared first. 

This makes it possible to identify whether the original publisher is a private owner or a real estate agent, and to distinguish them from intermediaries who later replicated the same advertisement. The result is a ranked list showing the original source first, followed by all subsequent copies with their respective publication dates.

##  **003-Información relativa a las soluciones**  {#003-información-relativa-a-las-soluciones}

**Parte 1:**

For this project, MySQL is used as the sole database. It stores all structured data — prices, IDs, number of rooms, square meters, areas, and other property-related fields. This type of information is stable, clearly defined, and straightforward to compare, making MySQL well suited for the core logic of the application.

Originally, ChromaDB was planned as a vector database for semantic description comparison. However, during development it became clear that GPT-4.1-mini could handle description comparison much more accurately and with less complexity, so ChromaDB was removed. MySQL handles all data storage, and the AI API handles the semantic layer.

**Parte 2:**

Both PHP and Python are used on the server side, each with a specific role.

PHP handles the web application — user interaction, forms, authentication, the admin panel, and all communication with the MySQL database. Python is used exclusively for web scraping and data processing. Scraping external websites is one of the more complex parts of the project, and Python's libraries for HTTP requests and HTML parsing make it the right tool for that job. The admin panel CRUD ended up being handled in PHP.

**Parte 3:**

On the client side, the project uses HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript — no frameworks. HTML provides the page structure, CSS handles all visual styling, and JavaScript adds interactivity such as form behaviour, the bilingual EN/ES language toggle, and the live crawler log polling in the admin panel.

##  **004-Aspectos innovadores**  {#004-aspectos-innovadores}

In my project, I use AI as a way to solve my assignment in a more modern and efficient way. The goal is not innovation for its own sake, but to use current technology to handle something that would otherwise require a lot of manual work and subjective judgement. I try to be as efficient as possible and not limit myself.

At the same time, I am aware that this kind of automation has a cost. Just like other AI-based solutions, it can reduce the need for certain manual tasks. In my case, the intention is not to replace professionals, but to support clearer analysis and reduce confusion by using AI as a practical tool within the system. 

##  **005-Estudio de viabilidad técnica**  {#005-estudio-de-viabilidad-técnica}

When comparing a normal web project with one that uses AI, the difference in cost and infrastructure is very clear. A simple blog or web application can run on a small server with around 2–4 GB RAM, 60–80 GB storage and a standard i3–i5 CPU. This usually costs between 3.60 € and 10–20 € per month, or around 6–12 € for typical student hosting. This setup is enough for traditional content, databases and normal user traffic.

When AI is added, the costs increase a lot. Running AI models often requires much more computing power, especially GPUs. In some cases, monthly costs can easily reach 20–50 €, and professional hardware like an RTX 4090 can cost around 250 € or more. This shows that AI can solve more complex problems, but it also makes the project more expensive and harder to maintain if it is not planned carefully.

In my project, this means AI has to be used in a smart way. Instead of running heavy AI processes all the time, data can be analysed once, stored, and reused later. This is similar to the SEO example, where a database is downloaded, analysed, and uploaded again, saving server resources. The focus is on balancing innovation with realistic costs, so the project stays technically advanced but still affordable. Therefore I first try to compare all of my data in sql and then when i have narrowed the matches, then i will use ai.

##  **006-Partes del proyecto**  {#006-partes-del-proyecto}

This project represents the final assignment of my first year in the DAM/DAW course. With this application, my goal is to show everything I have learned throughout the year by building something that goes beyond a simple example. The level of complexity and the amount of work put into the project are meant to justify the grade and reflect the knowledge acquired during the course.

In my project, I apply server-side programming using Python and PHP, combined with basic client-side programming, markup, and styling. The application stores data persistently in a database and includes both a user-facing front-end and an administration panel. The admin panel allows full CRUD operations, so I can create, read, update, and delete information, which demonstrates practical use of backend logic.

From a development and systems perspective, I document the project and upload it regularly to GitHub, making my progress visible through commits. The application is also designed to be able to be deployed on a server environment, such as a Windows Server, like we have done in class. Additionally, the front-end is planned to support at least two languages, which shows an understanding of internationalisation and real-world application requirements.

##  **008-Realización de presupuestos económicos** {#008-realización-de-presupuestos-económicos}

FirstListing is priced at 30 € per month, which equals 360 € per year per client.

The target market is Costa Blanca South, where there are approximately 850–900 active real estate agencies.

Development time for the current beta version has been roughly two and a half months. However, to reach real production value, an estimated additional two and a half months of work would be needed, bringing the total to approximately five months. Working an average of 1.5 hours per day over that period gives around 375 hours of development time. At a rate of 20 €/hour, the total development cost comes to 7,500 €.

First-year operating costs are estimated at 31,500 € — 24,000 € in salary and approximately 7,500 € in material costs (hardware, hosting, utilities).

To break even on operating costs alone, FirstListing needs approximately 88 paying clients (31,500 / 360 ≈ 88), which represents around 10% of the local market.

A more realistic first-year scenario would be 40–60 clients, generating between 14,400 € and 21,600 € — meaning a first-year loss is likely unless I do not take a full salary, which is a realistic possibility given the part-time nature of the project.

At 25% market penetration (around 225 agencies), annual revenue would reach approximately 81,000 €, which would comfortably cover all costs and generate profit.

##  **009-Documentación para el diseño**  {#009-documentación-para-el-diseño}

For a project like FirstListing, the design documentation process would go roughly like this.

It would start with an initial meeting or interview with the client to understand their needs. From there, communication would continue back and forth by email to confirm exactly what was discussed and agreed upon. This is important because it puts everything in writing — both parties know what is expected.

After that, a technical proposal and project memory would be created. In this case, that is essentially this document itself, covering the product overview and how it is built. Since the project is already largely complete, this would serve as a retrospective overview rather than a forward-looking plan.

Since FirstListing operates as a subscription service rather than a one-time delivery, the standard client contract is replaced by terms and conditions that the user accepts on registration. FirstListing already handles this through its Privacy Policy and Legal Notice, published on the website, which cover GDPR compliance and the legal framework required under Spanish law.The GDPR was reviewed to ensure the application's data handling is compliant.

Once the service is live and the client has started using it, an invoice would be issued for the agreed amount.

##  **010-Aspectos sobre la calidad del proyecto**  {#010-aspectos-sobre-la-calidad-del-proyecto}

For a project of this size developed by a single person, a full SCRUM or Kanban setup felt like overkill. Instead, quality and progress were managed through a combination of being an organised person and keeping a physical notebook. Writing down ideas, structures, and what needed to be done next was sufficient — it made it easy to sketch out timelines and think through how the different components should fit together, which was especially useful in the early stages.

Git was used throughout for tracking progress and maintaining code quality. Every meaningful change was committed with a message, making it possible to review the project history, roll back if something broke, and keep a clear record of what was done and when. One honest note — the commit messages are not always as descriptive as they should be, which is something to improve in future projects.

In terms of meeting objectives, the project had two fixed deadlines: the presentation on 27 February and the final delivery on 25 March. These acted as natural checkpoints that kept the work on track and forced each phase to reach a functional state before moving on.

Code quality was maintained through rigorous daily testing. After every function implemented, it was tested — first independently, then integrated with the rest of the system. Each major component, the crawler, the parser, the SQL scoring, and the AI comparison, was verified both in isolation and as part of the full pipeline.

A demo portal of five fake local listing pages was also built specifically for testing purposes. Since only one real agency website could legally be crawled, the demo portal provided a controlled set of known listings that could produce predictable and varied results, simulating how the crawler and duplicate detection would behave in a real scenario.

No formal Trello board or project management tool was used. With clear deadlines, a single developer, and regular commits, a notebook and Git served the same purpose effectively.

## **011-Presentación en público de las ideas más relevantes**  {#011-presentación-en-público-de-las-ideas-más-relevantes}

The public presentation of FirstListing took place as planned. The demo was run live rather than using slides, walking the audience through the application directly. The presentation covered the main purpose of the project, the duplicate detection pipeline, and the database structure, giving a solid overall overview of what the system does and how it works. The presentation also explained properly why I decided to make this specific project.

The main thing that didn't go as planned was time — the section on the crawler had to be cut short. Despite that, the presentation was well received and the audience came away with a clear understanding of the project.

## **012-Parámetros de igualdad** {#012-parámetros-de-igualdad}

After reviewing the full project, no gender inequalities or biases were identified.

FirstListing is a technical B2B tool for the real estate market. The interface is functional and task-oriented — users submit a URL and receive results. There is very little descriptive or narrative text in the product itself, which means there is limited opportunity for gendered language or biased framing to appear in the first place.

The user roles (agent, admin, private) are neutral and not tied to any gender assumptions. The AI prompts used for field extraction and description comparison are purely analytical — they compare prices, square meters, room counts, and property descriptions, with no personal or demographic data involved.

The registration system collects only a username, optional email, and password — no gender, name, or personal details are required or stored.

In conclusion, the project does not appear to reflect or perpetuate gender inequality in either its UI or its AI components.

# **003-Propuesta de empresa spin off** {#003-propuesta-de-empresa-spin-off}

## **000-Introducción al planteamiento de la empresa spin off** {#000-introducción-al-planteamiento-de-la-empresa-spin-off}

![][image2]

The spin-off company created to commercialize this product is called FirstListing. It is a small B2B software startup focused on the Spanish real estate market, offering a subscription-based web tool that detects duplicate property listings and identifies which portal published a listing first. The target clients are real estate agencies, primarily in coastal markets such as Costa Blanca South.

A logo was designed for the company using AI tools, combining a location pin and a bar chart to represent the core concept — tracking which listing appeared first across different portals. The visual identity is clean and professional, suited to a B2B product targeting real estate professionals.

The application itself serves as the landing page and product demo. Screenshots of the full interface are included in the [annexes](#001-firstlisting-interfaces).

##  **001-Temporalización de las secuencias de las actividades**  {#001-temporalización-de-las-secuencias-de-las-actividades}

Since this section was written in retrospect, here is what the timeline actually looked like.

Around 20 February, three weeks into the project, the system had its first rough shape. There was a basic crawler, a basic parser, and a first iteration of the MySQL database. Nothing was polished, but the core pipeline existed and could run.

Between that point and the partial delivery, the focus was on getting the crawler and parser to a state I was actually satisfied with, and building a basic but functional website on top of it. That was enough to present.

From the presentation through to the final delivery on 25 March, the work shifted to refinement. The website was upgraded, the code was cleaned up across several iterations, and both the crawler and parser received one more round of improvements. A significant part of that was reducing the token usage when calling the OpenAI API — at the time of the presentation it was consuming roughly 15,000 to 20,000 tokens per run, which was far too much. That got brought down considerably.

By 25 March the project was complete. The presentation had shown a working prototype, and everything done after that was the kind of detailed work that makes a project feel finished rather than just functional.

## **002-Determinación de recursos y logística de cada actividad** {#002-determinación-de-recursos-y-logística-de-cada-actividad}

For hardware, the entire project was developed on a personal MacBook Pro M3. No external server was needed at any point — the local development environment ran entirely on the machine itself via Homebrew, which handled Apache and MySQL locally.

On the software side, the main tools were a code editor. I used VScode, Python 3 for the crawler, PHP for the web application, and MySQL for the database. Git was used throughout for version control, with the repository hosted on GitHub as required.

The only external paid service used was the OpenAI API, specifically GPT-4.1-mini, which handled both the field extraction and the description comparison steps in the pipeline. The cost per run is minimal — roughly \$0.0003 per comparison call — so the total API cost across the whole project was negligible. All in all, I have spent only roughly 25 cents on API calls.

In terms of time, work was done intermittently over roughly two and a half months, averaging around 1.5 hours per day on active days. No office or external workspace was needed — the project was developed entirely from home or in class.

## **003-Permisos y autorizaciones necesarios** {#003-permisos-y-autorizaciones-necesarios}

FirstListing complies with GDPR by collecting only the minimum necessary data — username, optional email, bcrypt-hashed password, and search URLs. A full Privacy Policy and Legal Notice are published on the site, covering legal bases (GDPR Art. 6.1.b), retention, erasure rights, and OpenAI as the sole third-party processor.

No sector-specific regulation applies beyond standard GDPR, as the tool is aimed at private B2B users and not public administrations.

Crawling permission for the primary test site was obtained directly from the site owner, and the crawler uses a polite User-Agent and a 1.5-second delay between requests. The GDPR was reviewed to ensure the application's data handling is compliant.

##  **004-Actividades que implican riesgos**  {#004-actividades-que-implican-riesgos}

Even though FirstListing is a software business, there are still risks.

There are electrical risks if cables are badly installed. A 220V connection can cause serious injury or fire. Low voltage devices can cause small electric shocks. There is also the risk of losing equipment, which could mean loss of important data.

Ergonomic risks are very important. Long hours in front of a computer can cause back pain, eye strain, carpal tunnel syndrome, and even burnout. These problems can lead to sick leave and financial losses.

To reduce these risks, the company should ensure safe cable installation, regular data backups, and an ergonomic workspace with proper breaks.

##  **006-Recursos materiales y humanos de cada actividad**  {#006-recursos-materiales-y-humanos-de-cada-actividad}

Throughout the entire project, the only human resource was the developer — myself — handling everything from database design to frontend, crawler, AI integration, and documentation.

For the initial planning and database design phase, nothing special was needed beyond a pen and paper for sketching and a computer to work on.

During the core development phase, the resources were my MacBook Pro, a local Apache and MySQL environment running via Homebrew, Python 3, PHP, and the OpenAI API — used both for the parser and for the AI chat widget that explains the project to visitors.

The same setup covered the frontend and admin dashboard phases as well. No additional tools or services were needed at any point.

In short, the project required one developer, one personal computer, a local development stack, and the OpenAI API. No team, no office, no external server.

##  **007-Posibles imprevistos**  {#007-posibles-imprevistos}

The two weakest points in the system are the crawler and the parser, since they are by far the most complex parts of the project. If any of the target real estate websites were to change their HTML structure, it would force a problem immediately. This is also a challenge when trying to add new websites to the system — different sites have different structures, different amounts of raw text, and different JSON-LD implementations. This caused a lot of issues early in development and would likely be the main scaling problem if the project were to grow.

A second risk is the OpenAI API becoming unavailable or changing its pricing. The pipeline depends on it heavily, and as became clear early in the project, doing the parsing in pure Python without AI is at least very complicated. If the API went away, the core feature would break.

SQL injection and session hijacking are also risks worth mentioning. Since this is a school project running locally and not on a live server, the actual risk is low — but it is still something to be aware of. The project mitigates this through PDO with parameterized queries, bcrypt password hashing, and session-based authentication.

Data loss and data corruption are also possible. Raw HTML can grow large quickly, especially if the crawler starts capturing more of a page than intended. Currently each crawled page stores between 20,000 and 25,000 characters of HTML, but if the crawler scope widened that could easily reach 100,000 characters per page, which would create storage and performance problems.

Finally, token usage is a real risk. Early in development the parser was consuming between 15,000 and 20,000 tokens per run. That has since been reduced to between 2,000 and 5,000 tokens, but if the parser logic changed or new input types were added, that number could climb again.

Since the project runs locally rather than on a live server, traditional IT security measures such as firewall configuration and server updates are not directly applicable at this stage. However, if the project were deployed to a production environment, these would be standard requirements — keeping the server OS and dependencies updated, configuring a firewall, and setting up regular automated backups to prevent data loss.

## **008-Documentación necesaria** {#008-documentación-necesaria}

For a project like this, I would create two manuals: a developer manual and a user manual.

The developer manual would cover everything needed to set up and work on the project from scratch. This includes the system requirements, how to install and configure the local environment (Apache, MySQL, Python 3, PHP via Homebrew), how to set up the database using the provided SQL schema, and how to configure the OpenAI API key. It would also document the project structure, explain the four-step pipeline in detail, describe the database schema and the reasoning behind key design decisions, and outline how to run the crawler in both single-URL and sitemap bulk mode.

The user manual would be simpler and aimed at non-technical real estate agents. It would explain how to register and log in, how to submit a listing URL and understand the results, what the duplicate score means, what the AI confidence badges indicate, and what the known limitations of the system are — particularly that "first seen" refers to when the crawler first encountered the listing, not when it was originally published. It would be much different than the developer manual.

## **002-Transmisión de información horizontal y vertical**  {#002-transmisión-de-información-horizontal-y-vertical}

Since FirstListing is a B2B tool aimed at real estate professionals, the marketing strategy is more targeted than a general consumer product.

For online media, the most relevant channels are LinkedIn and direct outreach — either via LinkedIn messages or by finding phone numbers on agency websites and reaching out via WhatsApp. Having worked in the real estate sector, I know that email marketing tends to work less well than direct personal contact in this industry.

SEO and SEM are both important. A clean, professional landing page is essential — if I am approaching tech-averse real estate professionals and positioning myself as a tech solution, a poor website would immediately undermine credibility. It would be the first thing a potential client checks. SEM could be used later to accelerate visibility once the product is validated.

Instagram and Facebook have limited value for this audience. YouTube is more interesting than it might seem — many real estate agencies run YouTube channels, which makes it a useful ad targeting surface. TikTok is not relevant.

For offline marketing, direct outreach is the most practical approach. Agency locations are publicly listed online, so visiting offices in person combined with business cards would likely be more effective than any digital campaign at the local level.

The buyer persona is a real estate agent or agency owner, aged roughly 30 to 45, based in coastal Spain. The sweet spot is actually the back-office staff — the administrators who sit and create the listings, rather than the agents who do the selling. These are the people who deal with duplicate listings daily and would immediately understand the value of the product. They need to be moderately tech-savvy, which is why the younger end of the age range is the primary target. People over 60 in this sector tend to rely on word of mouth and established habits, making them harder to convert.

## **003- Instrucciones exposición del proyecto**

Exposición pública en la que:

\-Hay un tribunal generalmente compuesto por tres profesores (adicionalmente pueden asistir personas de dirección)

\-Opcionalmente se admite público (familia, conocidos, compañeros de clase)

Duración de la exposición:

Suele ser entre 15-20 minutos por persona

+ 5-10 minutos de preguntas del tribunal

Se puede traer:

1.-Botellita de agua (2 funciones, aclarar la garganta, balon de oxigeno)

2.-Sara bolsa para vomitar

3.-notas para apoyaros

Las notas son para lectura ocasional, NUNCA debéis hacer la exposición leyendo las notas

**Distribución del contenido (tiempo):**

Por redondear ejemplo 20 minutos

50% inicial \= mostrar la aplicación en funcionamiento

	10% \= Introducción al proyecto (si queréis power, en esta parte)

	40% \= aplicación tal y como la usaría un usuario final (nada de powerpoint, aplicación real en funcionamiento en la pantalla)

50% final \= mostrar el código y la base de datos

	40% \= las tripas de la aplicación

		20% programación (codigo limpio, comentado, claro, estructura clara de carpetas y archivos, todo bien nombrado, etc)

		20% de bases de datos o contenedores de información (modelo entendible, tablas bien nombradas, columnas bien nombradas, estructura legible y entendible, etc)

	10% \= cierre y conclusión

**Lenguaje no verbal:**

Se recomienda exponer de pie

Mirar al tribunal

Con respecto a lal creatividad \- Imagináos que no estáis en un tribunal de ciclo formativo sino en una entrevista en una empresa
